name: Stimmung
editorial_article:
"Stimmung" (1968) by Karlheinz Stockhausen stands as a monumental achievement in 20th-century avant-garde vocal music. Composed for six vocalists, the piece is a meditative, immersive exploration of overtone singing, grounded entirely on the overtones of a single fundamental B flat pitch. By focusing on the acoustic properties of the human voice, Stockhausen abandoned traditional melodic and harmonic progression in favor of a static, ritualistic exploration of sound itself. The work is structured into 51 interconnected "models," which transition fluidly, drawing the listener into an expansive sonic landscape that blends speech, chanting, and pure overtone resonance.

The title itself, a German word that translates to "tuning," "atmosphere," or "mood," perfectly encapsulates the piece’s intention: to bring the singers and listeners into a shared state of harmonic attunement. The vocalists are required to use vocal techniques—including throat singing and precise manipulation of vowel sounds—to isolate specific harmonics of the fundamental note. Throughout the performance, they chant names of deities from various global cultures, grounding the ethereal acoustic experiment in a sense of spiritual or secular mysticism. Since its premiere in Paris in 1968, "Stimmung" has remained a quintessential work of the European avant-garde, influencing countless minimalist and experimental composers by demonstrating the profound possibilities inherent in microtonal vocal performance. Various interpretations, such as the acclaimed recording by Paul Hillier and Theatre of Voices, have helped cement its status as a cornerstone of the modern repertoire, proving its continued relevance as a transformative experience for the listener.
editorial_teaser: A landmark of 20th-century avant-garde music, Karlheinz Stockhausen's "Stimmung" is a hypnotic, ritualistic composition for six voices based entirely on the overtones of a single fundamental pitch.
